verse.text: Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother,

to the assembly of God that is in Corinth, to those made holy in Christ Jesus, called to be holy ones, together with all who in every place call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, their Lord and ours:
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is always recognizable.

The verb is built on the ordinary word for “holy,” the same word that appears as “holy ones” later in this verse, and a Greek reader would have heard the link. Most translations use “sanctified”; the meaning is not in dispute, only the choice of English.

The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints,” but that word now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue, which is not what Paul means.
The Greek says only “theirs and ours.” Most interpreters attach this to “Lord,” as here. It could instead attach to “place” (“in every place, theirs and ours”).

verse.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
I always thank my God for you because of the grace of God that was given to you in Christ Jesus,
for in every way you were made rich in him, in all speech and all knowledge,
just as the testimony about Christ was firmly established among you,
so that you lack no gift as you eagerly await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ.
He will also keep you firmly established to the end, blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.
God is faithful, through whom you were called into fellowship with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

Now I urge you, brothers and sisters, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be knit together in the same mind and the same judgment.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as siblings, and Paul is addressing the whole community. Older translations have “brethren” or “brothers”; many recent ones use “brothers and sisters.”

verse.text: For Chloe’s people have made it clear to me, my brothers and sisters, that there are quarrels among you.
What I mean is this: each of you is saying, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” “I to Cephas,” “I to Christ.”

note.term: “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” “I to Cephas,” “I to Christ.”

verse.note: Cephas is the Aramaic name of Peter. Apollos was a teacher who worked in Corinth after Paul had founded the community there. Whether “I belong to Christ” was the slogan of a fourth group or is Paul’s own retort to the other three is disputed; the text here treats it as a fourth slogan, which is the more common view.

verse.text: Has Christ been divided up? Was it Paul who was crucified for you? Or were you baptized into the name of Paul?
I am thankful that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius,
verse.note: Many manuscripts read “I thank God” or “I thank my God.” The SBLGNT follows the shorter reading without “God,” found in some of the earliest witnesses; the longer forms are probably scribal expansions.

verse.text: so that no one can say that you were baptized into my name.
Well, I did also baptize the household of Stephanas; beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.
For Christ did not send me to baptize but to announce the good news, and not with wisdom of speech, so that the cross of Christ would not be emptied of its force.
verse.note: The Greek verb was an ordinary word for bringing or publicly announcing good news. “Gospel” is now a religious term or the name of a kind of book, so “good news” is used throughout; many modern translations do the same in places.

verse.text: For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.
For it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of those who understand I will set aside.”
Where is the wise person? Where is the scholar? Where is the debater of this age? Has God not made the wisdom of the world foolish?
verse.note: The word most likely refers here to the Jewish expert in the Scriptures, set beside the Greek “wise person.” The traditional “scribe” now suggests a copyist, whereas such a person was a trained interpreter and teacher. The line echoes Isaiah 33:18.

Older translations have “this world,” but the Greek is a time-word meaning an era. It reflects the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come. “World” at the end of the verse is a different Greek word (kosmos). Most modern translations also have “age” here.

verse.text: For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not come to know God through wisdom, God was pleased, through the foolishness of the proclamation, to save those who believe.
For Jews ask for signs and Greeks seek wisdom,
but we proclaim Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles,
verse.note: The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples” and in the plural was the standard Jewish term for the non-Jewish peoples; it is the same word translated “nations” elsewhere. Paul uses it interchangeably with “Greeks” in verses 22 and 24 as the counterpart to “Jews.”

verse.text: but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.
For what is foolish in God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak in God is stronger than human beings.
Consider your calling, brothers and sisters: not many of you were wise by human standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth.
verse.note: The Greek is literally “according to flesh,” meaning as measured in ordinary human terms. The same word appears in verse 29, where “no flesh” is a Semitic idiom for “no human being” and has been kept.

verse.text: But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise, and God chose what is weak in the world to shame what is strong,
and God chose what is lowborn in the world and what is despised, the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are,
so that no flesh may boast before God.
It is from him that you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and holiness and redemption,

note.term: and righteousness and holiness and redemption
note.traditional: and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption

verse.note: The Greek can be read as listing four things Christ became (wisdom, righteousness, holiness, redemption) or as explaining “wisdom” by the other three (“wisdom from God, that is, righteousness, holiness and redemption”). Many scholars favor the second reading; the text here keeps the looser “and” of the traditional rendering. “Holiness” translates a noun from the same family as “made holy” in verse 2, traditionally “sanctification.”

verse.text: so that, as it is written: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”
And I, when I came to you, brothers and sisters, did not come with superior speech or wisdom as I proclaimed to you the testimony of God.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole congregation. “Brothers and sisters” says in English what the first hearers understood. Many recent versions do the same, while others keep “brothers” with a footnote.

Some early and important manuscripts read “the secret of God” (traditionally “the mystery of God”) instead of “the testimony of God”; the two Greek words look alike. The evidence is closely balanced and editors are divided. The SBLGNT, followed here, reads “testimony”.

verse.text: For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
And I was with you in weakness and in fear and in much trembling,
and my speech and my proclamation were not with the persuasiveness of wisdom but with a demonstration of the Spirit and of power,
verse.note: The manuscripts differ considerably at this point. Many read “in persuasive words of wisdom,” which lies behind most English versions. The SBLGNT, followed here, adopts a shorter reading, literally “in persuasion of wisdom,” on the view that the longer forms are scribal expansions. The sense is hardly affected.

This was a standard term in rhetoric and philosophy for a compelling proof. Paul borrows the orators’ own vocabulary to say that the proof of his message came from the Spirit’s power, not from skill in argument or style.

verse.text: so that your faith might rest not on the wisdom of people but on the power of God.
Yet we do speak wisdom among the mature—a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing.
verse.note: The Greek word is a time-word meaning an era, here the present age as contrasted with the age to come. Older versions have “this world,” which blurs it with the different word for “world” in verse 12. Most modern versions also have “age” here.

These may be the human authorities who had Jesus put to death (see verse 8), or the spiritual powers thought to stand behind the present age, or both together. The word ordinarily means human rulers and officials, and many interpreters take it so here. Others see hostile spiritual powers. The translation leaves the question open.

verse.text: Rather, we speak God’s secret wisdom, the wisdom that has been hidden, which God decreed before the ages for our glory.

note.traditional: the wisdom of God in a mystery

verse.note: Most English versions keep “mystery,” understood as a truth once hidden and now revealed. In Jewish Greek of the period the word was the ordinary term for a secret, especially God’s hidden plan that only he can disclose, whereas English “mystery” now suggests a puzzle. The Greek is literally “God’s wisdom in a secret”. The phrase could instead go with the verb (“we speak, in a secret, God’s wisdom”), but most interpreters attach it to “wisdom”.

verse.text: None of the rulers of this age has known this wisdom; for if they had known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
But, as it is written: “What no eye has seen and no ear has heard, and what has not entered the human heart—all that God has prepared for those who love him.”
verse.note: The quotation matches no known passage of Scripture exactly. It is closest to Isaiah 64:4, perhaps blended with wording from Isaiah 65:17. Whether Paul is quoting freely, combining texts, or drawing on a form of the saying already in circulation is uncertain.

verse.text: For to us God has revealed them through the Spirit; for the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.
For who among people knows the things of a person except that person’s own spirit within? In the same way, no one has come to know the things of God except the Spirit of God.
Now we have not received the spirit of the world but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things freely given to us by God.
These things we also speak, not in words taught by human wisdom but in words taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual things to spiritual people.

note.term: interpreting spiritual things to spiritual people

verse.note: The Greek is compressed and disputed. The verb can mean “interpret,” “compare” or “combine,” and “spiritual” in the dative may refer to people or to things or words. Other defensible renderings are “comparing spiritual things with spiritual” and “explaining spiritual things in spiritual words”. The rendering here fits the contrast between kinds of people that follows in verses 14 and 15.

verse.text: A natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are examined spiritually.
verse.note: The Greek adjective comes from the word for “soul” or “life” and describes a person living by ordinary human life alone. Paul sets it against “spiritual,” meaning a person enlivened and taught by God’s Spirit. Some versions render it “unspiritual” or “the person without the Spirit”. “Natural” does not here mean unaffected or normal.

The same Greek verb occurs three times in verses 14 and 15. It means to examine, investigate or question, often of a judicial inquiry. Most versions vary the English (“discerned,” then “judges” and “is judged”), which hides the repetition. One rendering is kept here so that Paul’s play on the word can be heard.

verse.text: The spiritual person, however, examines all things, yet is himself examined by no one.
For “who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.

note.term: “who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him?”

verse.note: Paul quotes Isaiah 40:13 from the Greek version, which has “mind” where the Hebrew has “Spirit”. In Isaiah “the Lord” is God. Paul’s closing sentence sets “the mind of Christ” alongside it.

verse.text: And I, brothers and sisters, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as people of flesh, as infants in Christ.
verse.note: The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women. Paul is writing to the whole assembly at Corinth, so “brothers and sisters” says in English what the first hearers understood. Many recent translations do the same; others keep “brothers” and explain it in a footnote.

Paul uses two related adjectives. The one here means “made of flesh,” and the one in verse 3 (rendered “fleshly”) means “characterized by flesh,” that is, by ordinary human nature apart from God’s Spirit. The traditional “carnal” now suggests sexual sin, which is not the point; the failing in view is rivalry and faction. Scholars differ on how sharply the two adjectives should be distinguished, and some manuscripts interchange them.

verse.text: I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able to take it. Indeed, even now you are still not able,
for you are still fleshly. For where there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not fleshly and living in a merely human way?

note.term: living in a merely human way

verse.note: Literally “walking according to a human being.” “Walk” is a common biblical idiom for the way one conducts one’s life. “Merely” is supplied here and in verse 4, where the Greek is simply “are you not human beings?” The contrast with the “spiritual” people of verse 1 shows that Paul means human and nothing more.

verse.text: For when one says, “I belong to Paul,” and another, “I belong to Apollos,” are you not merely human?
What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? Servants through whom you came to believe, each as the Lord gave to him.
I planted, Apollos watered, but God was making it grow;
so neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God, who makes it grow.
The one who plants and the one who waters are one, and each will receive his own reward according to his own labor,
for we are God’s coworkers; you are God’s field, God’s building.

note.traditional: labourers together with God / God’s fellow workers

verse.note: The Greek can mean “those who work together with God” or “coworkers (with one another) who belong to God.” The rendering keeps the possessive form, which allows either sense and preserves the threefold “God’s … God’s … God’s” of the sentence. Many interpreters favor the second sense, because the context stresses that Paul and Apollos are servants and that God alone gives growth.

verse.text: According to the grace of God given to me, like a wise master builder I laid a foundation, and someone else is building on it. But let each one take care how he builds on it;
verse.note: “Wise” applied to a craftsman was normal Greek for “skilled,” and the same phrase occurs in the Greek version of Isaiah 3:3. The word is kept as “wise” because Paul is playing on the theme of wisdom that runs through these chapters. The “master builder” was the person who directed a building project on site, a different role from the modern architect.

verse.text: for no one can lay any foundation other than the one that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw,
each one’s work will become plain, for the day will make it clear, because it is revealed by fire; and the fire itself will test what kind of work each one has done.
verse.note: This is the day of the Lord, the expected day of God’s judgment, which Paul’s readers would have recognized without further explanation (compare 1:8). Fire is a standard prophetic image for that judgment. Here it is pictured as testing the materials of a building.

note.traditional: it shall be revealed by fire

verse.note: The subject of “is revealed” is not stated. Most interpreters take it to be the day, which arrives in fire; it could also be each person’s work, which is exposed by fire. The English “it” leaves the question as open as the Greek does.

verse.text: If the work anyone has built on it remains, he will receive a reward;
if anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire.
verse.note: The picture is of a builder who escapes through the flames of his own burning building: he gets out alive, but with nothing. Most interpreters understand it as a vivid image of a narrow escape. The verse was later drawn into discussions of purification after death, but the passage concerns the testing of the work of those who build up the community.

verse.text: Do you not know that you are God’s sanctuary and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?
verse.note: Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate “temple.” One names the whole complex with its courts. The one used here names the building where the deity dwells, and “sanctuary” keeps Paul’s image on that place. Most versions have “temple,” and “you are God’s temple” is deeply established in English. “You” is plural throughout: the community together is the one sanctuary.

verse.text: If anyone destroys God’s sanctuary, God will destroy that person; for God’s sanctuary is holy, and that is what you are.
Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become a fool so that he may become wise,
for the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight. For it is written: “He catches the wise in their craftiness,”

note.term: “He catches the wise in their craftiness,”

verse.note: The first quotation is Job 5:13, in wording that differs from the Septuagint as it has come down and stands closer to the Hebrew. The second, in verse 20, is Psalm 94:11 (93:11 in the Greek numbering). There the Psalm speaks of the thoughts “of people,” and Paul writes “of the wise” to fit his argument.

verse.text: and again: “The Lord knows the reasonings of the wise, that they are futile.”
So let no one boast in human beings. For all things are yours,
whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or things present or things to come—all are yours,
verse.note: Cephas is the Aramaic name, meaning “rock,” of the apostle better known by its Greek equivalent, Peter. Paul normally uses the Aramaic form. Cephas was one of the figures around whom factions in Corinth had formed (1:12).

verse.text: and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.
This is how a person should regard us: as servants of Christ and stewards of God’s secrets.
verse.note: Most English versions keep “mysteries” here as an established technical term. In Jewish Greek of the period the word was the ordinary term for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose. “Mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas Paul means things God has made known and entrusted to his stewards to pass on. A steward was a household manager, often a slave, answerable to the master for what was placed in his charge.

verse.text: Now what is looked for in stewards is this: that one be found faithful.
But to me it matters very little that I should be examined by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even examine myself.
verse.note: The Greek says literally “a human day.” Paul appears to coin the phrase as a counterpart to “the day of the Lord,” the day when God judges (see 3:13): a day of reckoning set by human beings. Most translations render the sense as “human court” or “human judgment,” as here.

verse.text: For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not vindicated by that; the one who examines me is the Lord.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “justified,” and some versions have “acquitted.” The verb belongs to the same Greek word-family as “righteous” and “righteousness,” which English splits between two sets of words. Here the setting is a judicial examination, and Paul’s point is that a clear conscience is not itself a verdict in his favor; only the Lord’s finding counts.

verse.text: So do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes. He will bring to light the things hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts, and then each one’s praise will come from God.

Now, brothers and sisters, I have applied these things to myself and Apollos for your sake, so that in us you may learn the saying “Not beyond what is written,” so that none of you will be puffed up in favor of one against another.
verse.note: The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women, as Paul’s assemblies were. “Brothers” alone would now be heard as excluding the women. Many modern translations make the same choice.

The verb elsewhere means to change the form or appearance of something. Here Paul seems to mean that he has cast his argument in terms of himself and Apollos as examples, perhaps tactfully avoiding naming the real offenders at Corinth. Some take it more simply as “I have used these figures of speech (farmers, builders, stewards) about myself and Apollos.”

note.traditional: not to go beyond what is written

verse.note: The Greek is a clipped phrase with no verb, introduced as if it were a known slogan or proverb. Most interpreters take “what is written” to mean Scripture, perhaps the passages Paul has quoted in chapters 1–3 against human boasting. Others suggest a general maxim about keeping to the rules, and a few suspect the text is damaged. The exact reference is uncertain.

verse.text: For who sets you apart? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you had not?
Already you have had your fill! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! And I wish you really had become kings, so that we too might be kings with you!
For it seems to me that God has put us apostles on display last, like people condemned to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels and to people.
verse.note: The word means a theater and, by extension, the show staged in it. Paul pictures the apostles as the condemned prisoners brought on last, either at the end of a victory procession or as the final act in the arena, where they were to die before the crowd. The audience here is the whole universe, heavenly and human.

verse.text: We are fools because of Christ, but you are sensible in Christ! We are weak, but you are strong! You are honored, but we are dishonored!
verse.note: Most translations have “wise.” The Greek word is not the one Paul uses for “wise” and “wisdom” throughout chapters 1–3; it means prudent, shrewd, having good sense. “Sensible” keeps the two words distinct. The tone is ironic, as in the rest of the verse.

verse.text: To this very hour we go hungry and thirsty, we are poorly clothed, we are beaten, we are homeless,
and we toil, working with our own hands. When we are insulted, we bless; when we are persecuted, we endure;
when we are slandered, we answer kindly. We have become like the scum of the world, the dirt scraped off everything, right up to now.

note.term: the scum of the world, the dirt scraped off everything
note.traditional: the filth of the world, the offscouring of all things

verse.note: The two Greek nouns both mean the dirt removed when something is scoured or wiped clean, and both were used as terms of abuse for worthless people. Some scholars think they also carried the sense of a person sacrificed as a scapegoat to purify a city, but the evidence that this was a live meaning in Paul’s day is disputed. The second phrase could also be read “the dirt scraped off everyone.”

verse.text: I am not writing these things to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children.
For even if you have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus it was I who fathered you through the good news.
verse.note: The word names a household slave who escorted a boy to and from school and supervised his conduct until he came of age. He was a minder and disciplinarian, not a teacher and certainly not a parent. Paul’s point is that the Corinthians may have any number of supervisors, but only one person brought them to life in Christ.

The traditional rendering is “gospel,” which is now a religious term or a book title. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between the two renderings.

verse.text: So I urge you: become imitators of me.
This is why I have sent Timothy to you. He is my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, and he will remind you of my ways in Christ Jesus, just as I teach everywhere in every assembly.
verse.note: “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering of citizens and as the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

verse.text: But some have become puffed up, as though I were not coming to you.
But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of those who are puffed up but their power,
for the kingdom of God is not in talk but in power.
What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?
verse.note: Older versions have “meekness,” which now suggests weakness; the Greek does not. The word describes a person who is not harsh or self-assertive. “Gentleness” is the mainstream modern rendering. “Spirit” here is most likely a disposition, though some take it as a reference to God’s Spirit.

verse.text: It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and sexual immorality of a kind not found even among the Gentiles: a man has his father’s wife.
verse.note: The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations” and is the same word rendered “nations” elsewhere in this translation; in the plural it regularly means the non-Jewish peoples. Paul is writing to a largely non-Jewish congregation, yet he uses the word for outsiders who do not know God.

“Father’s wife” is the wording of Leviticus 18:8 for a stepmother, as distinct from one’s own mother. “Has” indicates a continuing sexual relationship, whether marriage or cohabitation. Such a union was forbidden by Jewish law and by Roman law as well, which is the point of “not found even among the Gentiles.”

verse.text: And you are puffed up! Should you not rather have mourned, so that the one who did this deed would be removed from among you?
For I, absent in body but present in spirit, have already passed judgment, as if present, on the one who has done this in such a way:
in the name of our Lord Jesus, when you are gathered together, and my spirit with you, along with the power of our Lord Jesus,

note.term: in the name of our Lord Jesus
note.traditional: in the name of our Lord Jesus

verse.note: The sentence running through verses 3–5 is tangled in Greek, and it is unclear what this phrase attaches to. It may go with “I have passed judgment,” with “when you are gathered together,” or with “hand over”; a few scholars even attach it to “the one who has done this.” Likewise “with the power of our Lord Jesus” may describe the gathering or the handing over. The translation keeps the Greek order and leaves the connection open.

verse.text: you are to hand such a person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.
verse.note: Handing over to Satan means putting the man out of the community, into the realm where Satan holds sway. What “the destruction of the flesh” means is disputed: some take it as physical suffering or even death, others as the destruction of the man’s sinful orientation, “flesh” in Paul’s moral sense. The Greek says simply “the flesh” and “the spirit,” without “his,” and the translation keeps that.

note.traditional: the day of the Lord Jesus

verse.note: Many manuscripts read “the day of the Lord Jesus” or “the day of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and older English versions follow them. The shorter reading, found in some of the earliest witnesses, is the one printed in the Greek text translated here.

verse.text: Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole batch of dough?
Clean out the old leaven so that you may be a new batch, just as you are in fact unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
verse.note: Leaven was a lump of fermented dough kept back from an earlier batch to raise the next one. Before Passover every Jewish household removed all leaven from the home, and for the seven days of the festival only unleavened bread was eaten (Exodus 12:15–20). Paul builds the whole image of verses 6–8 on this practice.

The Greek has only “our Passover.” The word can mean the festival, the meal, or the animal slaughtered for it; with the verb “sacrificed” it means the lamb, and most modern translations add the word for clarity.

verse.text: So let us keep the festival, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people—
verse.note: Paul refers to an earlier letter to Corinth, written before 1 Corinthians, which has not survived. The Corinthians had evidently taken its instruction to mean avoiding all immoral people, which Paul now corrects.

verse.text: not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and robbers, or idolaters, since then you would have to leave the world.

But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who is called a brother if he is sexually immoral or greedy, or an idolater, a reviler, a drunkard, or a robber—not even to eat with such a person.
verse.note: The Greek verb is a past tense, which letter writers often used of the letter in hand. The phrase can also be read “But as it is, what I wrote was,” making this a clarification of what the earlier letter meant, not a fresh instruction. Either way the point is the same: the ban concerns members of the community, not outsiders.

verse.text: For what business is it of mine to judge those outside? Do you not judge those inside,
while God judges those outside? “Remove the wicked person from among yourselves.”
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts were written without accents, and the same letters can be read as a present (“judges”) or a future (“will judge”). The Greek text translated here prints the present; many translations and commentators prefer the future.

note.term: “Remove the wicked person from among yourselves.”
note.traditional: Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person.

verse.note: Paul closes with words from a refrain that recurs in Deuteronomy (for example 17:7; 22:21, 24), quoted from the Greek version with the verb changed to the plural. He gives no introductory formula, but the wording is recognizably scriptural. In Deuteronomy the refrain follows capital offenses; here Paul applies it to exclusion from the community.

verse.text: Does any of you who has a dispute with another dare to go to law before the unjust and not before the holy ones?
verse.note: Greek has one word family where English has two (“just” and “righteous,” “justice” and “righteousness,” “justify”). Paul plays on it through this passage: believers sue before “the unjust” (v. 1), should rather “suffer injustice” (v. 7), in fact “inflict injustice” (v. 8), are warned that “the unjust” will not inherit the kingdom (v. 9), and are reminded that they were “justified” (v. 11). Most translations vary the English (“unrighteous,” “wronged,” “do wrong”), which hides the thread. Here the term labels outsiders to the community, as “unbelievers” does in verse 6.

The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of unusual virtue. Paul uses the word for all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people” or “the Lord’s people.”

verse.text: Or do you not know that the holy ones will judge the world? And if the world is judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the most trivial cases?
Do you not know that we will judge angels—to say nothing of everyday matters?
So if you have cases about everyday matters, is it those who count for nothing in the assembly that you seat as judges?
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout.

note.term: is it those who count for nothing in the assembly that you seat as judges?
note.traditional: set them to judge who are least esteemed in the church

verse.note: The Greek verb can be read as a question, a statement, or a command. As a question, it rebukes the Corinthians for taking cases to pagan judges, who have no standing in the community. As a command, as in the King James Version, it is ironic: even the least regarded believers would be fit to judge such trivial matters. Most recent translations and commentators take it as a question.

verse.text: I say this to shame you. Is it really so, that there is not one wise person among you who will be able to decide between one brother and another,
but brother goes to law against brother—and this before unbelievers?
In fact, it is already an utter defeat for you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why not rather suffer injustice? Why not rather be defrauded?
Instead, you yourselves inflict injustice and defraud—and you do this to brothers and sisters!

Or do you not know that the unjust will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who take the passive role with men, nor men who bed males,

note.term: men who take the passive role with men

verse.note: The Greek word literally means “soft.” Used of men it was a common term of contempt for effeminacy, and in sexual contexts it was applied to the passive partner in sex between males, often a youth. Because it stands in a list of sexual offenses beside the following term, most scholars take the sexual sense here. Older versions have “effeminate,” some have “male prostitutes,” and several merge the two terms into one phrase; the exact scope is disputed.

note.traditional: abusers of themselves with mankind; sodomites; homosexuals

verse.note: This rare word is first attested here and may be Paul’s coinage. It joins the words for “male” and “bed,” which stand side by side in the Greek version of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, and most scholars think it was formed from those verses to mean a man who has sex with males. The rendering “homosexuals” brings in a modern category of orientation, whereas the Greek word names an act. Some scholars argue for a narrower reference, such as exploitative sex or pederasty, and the evidence from later usage is thin.

verse.text: nor thieves, nor the greedy—no drunkards, no revilers, no robbers—will inherit the kingdom of God.
And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, but you were made holy, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and in the Spirit of our God.
verse.note: The Greek verb is built directly on the ordinary word for “holy,” the same word rendered “holy ones” in verses 1–2, and “made holy” keeps that link audible. “Sanctified,” used by most translations, now suggests to many readers a doctrine of gradual moral improvement, whereas Paul here speaks of a completed transfer into what belongs to God. The meaning itself is not in dispute.

verse.text: “Everything is permitted for me,” but not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permitted for me,” but I will not be mastered by anything.

note.traditional: All things are lawful unto me

verse.note: Most scholars think Paul is here quoting a slogan current among the Corinthians and then qualifying it, and most modern translations use quotation marks. The Greek has no such marks, so this is an inference from the way the sayings are repeated and corrected (compare 10:23). The same applies to the saying about food in verse 13, where it is disputed whether the slogan ends at “food” or continues through “the one and the other.”

verse.text: “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food,” and God will do away with both the one and the other. But the body is not for sexual immorality but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.
verse.note: The verb means to put something out of operation or bring it to an end, and it is not the ordinary Greek word for destroying. Many translations have “destroy” here. The point is that food and the stomach belong to a temporary order that God will end, in contrast with the body, which God will raise (v. 14).

The Greek word covers unlawful sexual intercourse of any kind and is broader than the older English “fornication.” It shares a root with the word for “prostitute” in verses 15–16 and with “the sexually immoral” in verse 9, so a Greek reader heard one connected set of words through the whole passage.

verse.text: And God both raised the Lord and will raise us up through his power.
Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? By no means!
verse.note: The Greek word means a limb or organ of a body, and “members” is used here in that sense, not in the sense of belonging to a group. Paul’s argument depends on the physical image: a believer’s body is a body part of Christ and so cannot be made a body part of a prostitute.

verse.text: Or do you not know that whoever is joined to a prostitute is one body with her? For it says, “The two will become one flesh.”
But whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him.
Flee from sexual immorality. Every sin that a person commits is outside the body, but the one who commits sexual immorality sins against his own body.

note.term: Every sin that a person commits is outside the body
note.traditional: Every sin that a man doeth is without the body

verse.note: The Greek says “every sin,” not “every other sin,” though many translations supply “other” so that the sentence states a general rule to which sexual sin is the exception. Some scholars instead take the sentence as another Corinthian slogan, claiming that sin does not touch the body, which Paul then contradicts. The rendering here leaves both readings open.

verse.text: Or do you not know that your body is a sanctuary of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? And you are not your own,
verse.note: Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the building where the deity dwells. “Sanctuary” keeps Paul’s image focused on the dwelling place of God’s Spirit. Most versions have “temple” here, and “your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit” is deeply established in English.

verse.text: for you were bought at a price. So glorify God in your body.
verse.note: The language is that of a purchase in the marketplace, and in a city like Corinth a reader would naturally think of the buying of a slave, who then belonged to the new owner. Paul uses the same phrase in 7:23. He does not say here what the price was or to whom it was paid.

verse.text: Now concerning the matters you wrote about: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.”

note.term: It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman

verse.note: Greek manuscripts have no quotation marks. Most recent scholars take this sentence as a statement from the Corinthians’ letter, which Paul quotes and then qualifies in the verses that follow. The older view reads it as Paul’s own opinion. The text follows the first view and marks the sentence as a quotation.

The Greek says “to touch a woman,” an established euphemism for sexual intercourse, found also in the Septuagint (for example Genesis 20:6). A modern reader could take “touch” to mean any physical contact, so the sense is given directly. Several recent translations do the same.

verse.text: But because of cases of sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife, and each woman should have her own husband.
The husband should give his wife what is owed to her, and likewise the wife to her husband.
The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; and likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.

Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer and then be together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.
I say this as a concession, not as a command.
I wish that all people were as I myself am. But each has their own gift from God, one of one kind and another of another.
To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them if they remain as I also am.
But if they are not exercising self-control, they should marry, for it is better to marry than to burn.
verse.note: The Greek has only the verb “to burn.” Most interpreters understand it as burning with sexual desire, which fits the mention of self-control, and many translations add “with passion.” A minority take it as burning in judgment.

verse.text: To the married I give this charge—not I, but the Lord—that a wife must not separate from her husband;
verse.note: Paul is referring to a teaching of Jesus on divorce, of the kind preserved in the Gospels (for example Mark 10:2–12). In verse 12 he has no such saying to cite and gives his own instruction. The two verbs here, “separate” and “divorce,” were both used for ending a marriage; the ancient world did not distinguish legal separation from divorce.

verse.text: but if she does separate, she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband—and that a husband must not divorce his wife.
To the rest I say—I, not the Lord—that if any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, he must not divorce her.
And if any woman has an unbelieving husband and he consents to live with her, she must not divorce her husband.
For the unbelieving husband has been made holy through his wife, and the unbelieving wife has been made holy through the brother. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is they are holy.
verse.note: The Greek verb is built on the ordinary word for “holy,” the same word used of the children at the end of the verse; “made holy” keeps that link visible where the traditional “sanctified” hides it. Paul does not mean the unbelieving spouse is saved (see verse 16). The point seems to be that the marriage does not defile the believer but brings the family within the sphere of what belongs to God, though the exact sense is debated.

verse.text: But if the unbeliever separates, let him separate. The brother or the sister is not enslaved in such cases; God has called us to peace.
For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?
Only, let each one walk as the Lord has apportioned to each, as God has called each. This is what I direct in all the assemblies.
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the one Greek word is recognizable.

verse.text: Was anyone called when already circumcised? He should not reverse his circumcision. Has anyone been called while uncircumcised? He should not be circumcised.
verse.note: The verb refers to a known procedure by which some Jewish men sought to restore the appearance of a foreskin, usually to avoid ridicule when exercising naked in Greek society. 1 Maccabees 1:15 mentions the practice.

verse.text: Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing; what matters is keeping God’s commandments.
Each person should remain in the calling in which they were called.
Were you called as a slave? Do not let it trouble you. But if you can in fact become free, by all means take the opportunity.

note.term: by all means take the opportunity

verse.note: The Greek says only “rather make use,” with no object. Most modern interpreters supply “freedom”: a slave who can gain freedom should take it. Many ancient and some modern interpreters supply “slavery”: even if you can become free, make the most of your present condition. The grammar allows both, and the text follows the majority view.

verse.text: For the one who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freed person; likewise the one who was called as a free person is Christ’s slave.
You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings.
Brothers and sisters, each one should remain with God in the condition in which they were called.
Now concerning the virgins, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is faithful.
I think, then, that this is good in view of the present distress: that it is good for a person to remain just as they are.
verse.note: The participle can mean “present” or “impending,” so some translations have “the impending crisis.” It is also disputed whether Paul means a local hardship in Corinth, the general pressures on believers, or the troubles expected before the end (compare verses 29–31).

verse.text: Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife.
But if you do marry, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet such people will have affliction in the flesh, and I am trying to spare you.
verse.note: The Greek word is an ordinary term for hardship that presses on a person. This translation renders it “affliction” throughout, so that the reader can see the same word wherever it occurs. Most versions here have “trouble” or “distress.”

verse.text: What I mean is this, brothers and sisters: the time has been cut short. From now on, even those who have wives should be as though they had none,
those who weep as though they were not weeping, those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, those who buy as though they owned nothing,
and those who make use of the world as though they were not making full use of it. For the form of this world is passing away.
I want you to be free from concern. The unmarried man is concerned about the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord.
But the married man is concerned about the things of the world, how he may please his wife,

and he is divided. Both the unmarried woman and the virgin are concerned about the things of the Lord, so as to be holy in both body and spirit. But the married woman is concerned about the things of the world, how she may please her husband.

note.traditional: There is difference also between a wife and a virgin

verse.note: The manuscripts differ in wording and punctuation across verses 33–34. One form of the text, followed by the King James Version, begins a new sentence here: “There is a difference also between the wife and the virgin.” The reading translated here, in which the married man is “divided,” is the one adopted in modern critical editions.

verse.text: I say this for your own benefit, not to throw a noose over you, but to promote what is proper and undistracted devotion to the Lord.
But if anyone thinks he is behaving improperly toward his betrothed, if his passions are strong and so it has to be, let him do what he wishes; he is not sinning. Let them marry.
verse.note: The Greek says literally “his virgin.” The text follows most recent translations in taking verses 36–38 to address a man and the woman he is engaged to. The older view, still defended, is that Paul addresses a father deciding whether to give his daughter in marriage; in its favor, the verb in verse 38 normally means “give in marriage” rather than “marry.” The choice affects the rendering of all three verses.

note.traditional: if she pass the flower of her age

verse.note: The Greek adjective is rare, and the verb has no expressed subject. It may describe the woman as past the usual age for marriage, or the man as having strong sexual desire. The text takes the second, which fits the contrast with the man in verse 37 who is under no compulsion, but the evidence does not settle the question.

verse.text: But the one who stands firm in his heart, who is under no compulsion but has authority over his own will, and has decided in his own heart to keep his betrothed as she is, will do well.
So the one who marries his betrothed does well, and the one who does not marry will do better.
A wife is bound for as long as her husband lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whomever she wishes, only in the Lord.
But in my judgment she is more blessed if she remains as she is—and I think that I too have the Spirit of God.
Now concerning food sacrificed to idols: we know that “we all have knowledge.” Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.
verse.note: In a Greek city most animals were slaughtered as sacrifices at temples. Part of the meat was eaten at meals in temple dining rooms, and part could be sold in the market. Sharing such meals was an ordinary part of social life, so the question touched family, business and civic ties. The Greek term is a Jewish and Christian one; pagans themselves spoke of “sacred” meat.

note.traditional: we know that we all have knowledge

verse.note: Greek manuscripts have no quotation marks. Most scholars think Paul is here quoting a slogan of some Corinthians, perhaps from their letter to him, and then qualifying it; the same applies to the statements in verse 4. It is also possible to read these words as Paul’s own statement.

verse.text: If anyone thinks they have come to know something, they do not yet know as they ought to know;
but if anyone loves God, that person is known by him.

note.term: that person is known by him
note.traditional: the same is known of him

verse.note: A few early witnesses, including the oldest papyrus of Paul’s letters, lack “God” and “by him”, giving “if anyone loves, that person is known” or possibly “has come to know”. Most manuscripts and editions have the longer text translated here.

verse.text: So then, concerning the eating of food sacrificed to idols: we know that “no idol in the world really exists,” and that “there is no God but one.”

note.term: no idol in the world really exists
note.traditional: an idol is nothing in the world

verse.note: The Greek can be read either as “there is no idol in the world”, meaning that the god an image represents has no real existence, or as “an idol is nothing in the world”. The first reading matches the parallel clause that follows (“there is no God but one”) and is followed here; the second is the traditional rendering and is also defensible.

verse.text: For even if there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—
yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom all things come and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things come and through whom we exist.
verse.note: The language of “one God” and “one Lord” echoes Israel’s daily confession, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4), where the Greek version has both “God” and “Lord”. Many scholars think Paul is deliberately restating that confession so that it includes Jesus Christ.

verse.text: But not everyone has this knowledge. Some, having been accustomed to idols until now, eat it as food sacrificed to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.
verse.note: Many later manuscripts read a similar-looking Greek word meaning “conscience” instead of “custom”, which is the source of the King James wording. The earliest witnesses read “custom” or “habit”, and modern editions and translations follow them.

verse.text: But food will not bring us near to God: we are no better off if we eat, and no worse off if we do not.
verse.note: The verb means to present or place someone before another. It may mean here that food does not bring a person close to God or win his approval, or, in a courtroom sense, that food will not bring a person before God for judgment. Either way the point is that eating or not eating makes no difference to one’s standing with God.

verse.text: But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak.
For if someone sees you, the one with knowledge, reclining at a meal in an idol’s temple, will not the conscience of that person, who is weak, be built up to eat food sacrificed to idols?
verse.note: Most translations have “emboldened” or “encouraged”. The Greek verb is the same one used in verse 1, “love builds up”, and Paul’s reuse of it is ironic: the knowledgeable person’s example does “build up” the weak person, but toward ruin. The rendering keeps that echo.

verse.text: For the weak person is being destroyed by your knowledge—the brother or sister for whom Christ died.
verse.note: The Greek word is the masculine “brother”, which in early Christian usage referred to any fellow believer, male or female. Many recent translations render it inclusively, as here, while others keep “brother”.

verse.text: And so, by sinning against your brothers and sisters and striking their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.
Therefore, if food causes my brother or sister to stumble, I will never eat meat again, so that I do not cause my brother or sister to stumble.

note.term: causes my brother or sister to stumble

verse.note: The King James Version has “offend”, which now suggests hurt feelings. The verb means to trip someone up so that they fall in their loyalty to God. Modern versions divide between “cause to stumble” and “cause to sin” or “cause to fall”; the first keeps both the picture and the breadth of the Greek.

verse.text: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord?
If to others I am not an apostle, to you at least I am, for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.
This is my defense to those who are examining me.
verse.note: “Defense” and “examining” are courtroom words: a formal reply to a charge and a preliminary judicial inquiry. “This” most likely points forward to the argument of verses 4–27, though some take it as pointing back to verses 1–2, with the Corinthians themselves as Paul’s defense.

verse.text: Do we have no right to eat and drink?
verse.note: The Greek word means authority or entitlement to do something. It is the same word used in 8:9 for the Corinthians’ “right” to eat food offered to idols. Paul’s whole chapter is an example of holding a real right and choosing not to use it.

verse.text: Do we have no right to take along a believing wife, as the other apostles and the Lord’s brothers and Cephas do?

note.traditional: a believing wife; a sister, a wife (KJV)

verse.note: The Greek is literally “a sister, a wife,” that is, a wife who is a fellow believer. Some ancient interpreters took it instead as “a sister as a woman,” a female assistant and not a spouse, but most scholars today read it as a wife who travels with her husband at the churches’ expense.

verse.text: Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right not to work?
Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit? Who shepherds a flock and does not have some of the flock’s milk?
Am I saying these things from a merely human point of view, or does the Law not say them too?
For in the Law of Moses it is written: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing.” Is it oxen that God is concerned about,

note.term: You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing.

verse.note: The quotation is Deuteronomy 25:4. Oxen threshed grain by treading it or dragging a sledge over it, and the law let the working animal eat as it went. Paul argues from the lesser to the greater: if this holds for an ox, it holds for human workers.

verse.text: or is it surely for our sake that he says it? Yes, it was written for our sake, because the one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes to thresh in hope of a share.
verse.note: The adverb can mean “entirely,” which would have Paul deny that the law is about oxen at all. It can also mean “surely” or “certainly,” which says only that its application to people is beyond doubt. The second sense is the commoner one in the period and is followed here, but both are defended.

verse.text: If we sowed spiritual things for you, is it too much if we reap material things from you?

If others share this right over you, do we not all the more? But we have not made use of this right. Instead we put up with everything, so that we may put no obstacle in the way of the good news of Christ.
verse.note: “Gospel” is now a religious term or the name of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for the public announcement of good news, and the related verb in verses 16 and 18 is rendered “announce the good news.” Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

verse.text: Do you not know that those who perform the temple service eat what comes from the temple, and those who attend to the altar share in what is offered on the altar?
In the same way the Lord also directed that those who proclaim the good news should live from the good news.
verse.note: Paul is referring to a teaching of Jesus preserved in the Gospels, that the worker deserves his pay or his food (Luke 10:7; Matthew 10:10). It is one of the few places where Paul explicitly appeals to a saying of Jesus.

verse.text: But I have made use of none of these things. And I am not writing this so that it may be done that way in my case, for I would rather die than— No one will make my boast an empty one!

note.term: than— No one will make my boast an empty one!
note.traditional: than that any man should make my glorying void

verse.note: In the earliest manuscripts Paul’s sentence breaks off and restarts, which is reproduced here. Many later manuscripts smooth it into a single clause, “than that anyone should make my boast empty,” and most English versions translate that smoother sense.

verse.text: For if I announce the good news, there is no boast in that for me, for necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not announce the good news!
For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship.

note.term: I have been entrusted with a stewardship
note.traditional: a stewardship; a commission; a dispensation (KJV)

verse.note: A steward was a household manager, very often a slave, who carried out his master’s business as a duty and earned no wages for it. Paul’s point seems to be that, since he preaches under compulsion, he is in that position and cannot claim pay. The logic and punctuation of verses 17–18 are disputed, and some read this clause as leading into the question that follows.

verse.text: What then is my reward? That in announcing the good news I may offer the good news free of charge, and so not make full use of my right in the good news.
For though I am free from all, I made myself a slave to all, so that I might win more of them.
To the Jews I became like a Jew, to win Jews. To those under the law I became like one under the law—though I myself am not under the law—to win those under the law.

note.term: though I myself am not under the law

verse.note: This clause is absent from many later manuscripts and so from the King James Version. It is present in the earliest and best witnesses, and was probably dropped by accident because of the repeated phrase “under the law.”

verse.text: To those outside the law I became like one outside the law—though I am not outside God’s law but within Christ’s law—to win those outside the law.

note.traditional: under the law of Christ; under law toward Christ

verse.note: Paul plays on two adjectives built on the word for law: “lawless” or “outside law” and “within law.” The phrase can be read as “subject to the law of Christ” or more loosely as “bound by law to Christ.” What Paul means by Christ’s law is debated; compare Galatians 6:2.

verse.text: To the weak I became weak, to win the weak. I have become all things to all people, so that by all means I might save some.
I do everything for the sake of the good news, so that I may share in it with others.

note.traditional: share in its blessings; be partaker thereof with you

verse.note: The Greek is literally “a fellow sharer of it.” Most translations take this as sharing in the blessings the good news brings. Others understand it as being a partner in the work of the good news itself. The rendering leaves both open.

verse.text: Do you not know that the runners in a stadium all run, but only one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you take hold of it.
Everyone who competes exercises self-control in everything. They do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable one.
verse.note: The prize at Greek athletic contests, including the Isthmian Games held near Corinth, was a wreath of foliage that soon withered. Elsewhere this translation renders the word “crown,” but here Paul’s contrast depends on the prize being literally perishable. Several modern versions make the same choice in this verse.

verse.text: So this is how I run: not aimlessly; this is how I box: not beating the air.
Rather, I pummel my body and make it my slave, so that after proclaiming to others I myself will not somehow be disqualified.

note.traditional: I discipline my body; I keep under my body (KJV)

verse.note: The verb comes from boxing and means to strike someone under the eye, to give a black eye. It continues the image of verse 26: Paul’s punches land, and they land on his own body. “Discipline” gives the application but loses the picture. “Disqualified” likewise continues the athletic image, of a competitor who fails the test.

verse.text: For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers and sisters, that our ancestors were all under the cloud and all passed through the sea,
and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,
and all ate the same spiritual food,
and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.

note.term: a spiritual rock that followed them

verse.note: Israel is given water from a rock near the start of the wilderness journey (Exodus 17) and again near its end (Numbers 20). Jewish interpreters of the period spoke of a well or rock that traveled with the people, and Paul appears to draw on that tradition, identifying the source of the water with Christ.

verse.text: But God was not pleased with most of them, for they were laid low in the wilderness.
Now these things happened as examples for us, so that we would not be people who crave evil, as they also craved.
verse.note: The Greek word means a pattern, model or mold. Some interpreters take it more strongly here as “types”, meaning events designed to prefigure the situation of Paul’s readers. Others take it simply as warning examples. The related adverb in verse 11 is rendered the same way.

verse.text: Do not become idolaters, as some of them were; as it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to revel.”
verse.note: The quotation is Exodus 32:6, from the golden calf episode. The verb covers playing, dancing and festive merrymaking; “play” is the traditional rendering, but in modern English it suggests children’s games, where the scene is one of celebration around an idol.

verse.text: Let us not commit sexual immorality, as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day.
verse.note: The reference is to the episode at Baal of Peor in Numbers 25, where the Hebrew and Greek texts both give twenty-four thousand. The reason for Paul’s figure is not known; proposed explanations include a slip of memory, a round number, or a different tradition, and none is certain.

verse.text: Let us not put Christ to the test, as some of them tested him, and were destroyed by the snakes.
verse.note: Some important early manuscripts read “the Lord” here, and a few read “God”. “Christ” is the reading of the edition translated and is widely thought more likely to be original, since copyists would have found it harder to speak of Israel in the wilderness testing Christ.

verse.text: And do not grumble, as some of them grumbled, and were destroyed by the destroyer.
Now these things were happening to them as examples, and they were written down to warn us, on whom the ends of the ages have come.
So anyone who thinks they are standing should watch out that they do not fall.

No testing has overtaken you that is not common to humanity. And God is faithful: he will not let you be tested beyond what you are able, but with the testing he will also provide the way out, so that you are able to endure it.
verse.note: Most English versions have “temptation” and “tempted” in this verse. The Greek noun and its verb mean a putting to the proof, and in the Greek Old Testament they are the usual words for Israel’s trials in the wilderness, which Paul has just recalled. Scholars disagree whether trial or enticement to sin is in view here; the two overlap, since the testing in question is pressure to join in idolatry.

verse.text: Therefore, my dear friends, flee from idolatry.
I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say.
The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ?
verse.note: The older tradition has “communion”, and many modern versions have “participation” or “sharing”. The Greek word means having something in common, here taking part in a thing together. The related noun in verses 18 and 20 is rendered “sharers” so that the link in Paul’s argument stays visible.

verse.text: Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
Look at Israel according to the flesh: are not those who eat the sacrifices sharers in the altar?
What then am I saying? That food sacrificed to an idol is anything, or that an idol is anything?
No, but that what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God, and I do not want you to become sharers with demons.

note.traditional: the things which the Gentiles sacrifice

verse.note: Many manuscripts name the subject, “the Gentiles”; the edition translated omits it as a probable clarifying addition. The sense is the same either way: “they” are the pagan worshipers, not Israel of verse 18. The wording echoes Deuteronomy 32:17.

verse.text: You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.
Or are we provoking the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he is?
“Everything is permitted”—but not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permitted”—but not everything builds up.
verse.note: Most scholars think Paul is quoting a slogan current at Corinth, which he then qualifies, and the quotation marks reflect that view. Greek manuscripts have no quotation marks, so the words can also be read as Paul’s own statement. The same saying appears at 6:12.

verse.text: Let no one seek their own good, but the good of the other person.
Eat everything sold in the meat market without raising any question on account of conscience,
for “the earth is the Lord’s, and all that fills it.”
If one of the unbelievers invites you and you want to go, eat everything set before you without raising any question on account of conscience.
But if someone says to you, “This was offered in sacrifice,” do not eat it, on account of the one who told you and on account of conscience.

note.traditional: This is offered in sacrifice unto idols

verse.note: The speaker uses the ordinary, respectful Greek term for meat from a temple sacrifice, not the disparaging “sacrificed to an idol” of verse 19; this is how a pagan, or someone speaking in a pagan’s house, would put it. Later manuscripts replace it with the “idol” word and repeat the quotation from verse 26 at the end of the verse.

verse.text: By conscience I mean not your own but the other person’s. For why should my freedom be judged by another’s conscience?
If I partake with thanks, why am I slandered over what I give thanks for?
verse.note: The Greek word can mean grace or thanks. Older versions read “by grace”, but most modern translators take it as thankfulness, because it is picked up at once by the related verb “give thanks”, referring to the prayer said over a meal.

verse.text: So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.
Give no cause for stumbling to Jews or to Greeks or to the assembly of God,
verse.note: “Church” is the near-universal rendering, and readers know what it refers to. The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Greek Old Testament’s word for Israel assembled before God. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation because “church” now suggests a building or an institution.

verse.text: just as I also try to please everyone in everything, not seeking my own benefit but that of the many, so that they may be saved.
Be imitators of me, just as I am of Christ.
I praise you because you remember me in everything and hold fast to the traditions just as I handed them on to you.
But I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of a woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for the head of the body, and its figurative force here is long disputed. Most lexical studies favor a sense of authority or preeminence; others argue for “source,” pointing to verses 8 and 12, where woman is “from” man. The translation keeps “head” because Paul plays on the literal and figurative senses through verse 10, so that “shames his head” in verse 4 can mean his own head, Christ, or both.

note.term: the head of a woman is the man
note.traditional: the head of the woman is the man

verse.note: Greek uses one word for “man” and “husband” and one for “woman” and “wife.” Some versions render “the head of a wife is her husband” and read the passage as concerning married couples. The translation keeps “man” and “woman” throughout because verses 8–9 and 12 argue from creation and birth, but the marital sense may be in view in places.

verse.text: Every man who prays or prophesies with something on his head shames his head;
verse.note: The Greek is literally “having down from the head.” Most interpreters take it as a covering hanging over the head, such as the fold of a garment that Roman men drew up when offering sacrifice. Some take it instead as long hair hanging down, in line with verse 14.

verse.text: but every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered shames her head, for it is one and the same thing as having her head shaved.
For if a woman does not cover herself, let her also have her hair cut off. But if it is disgraceful for a woman to have her hair cut off or to be shaved, let her cover herself.
For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of man.
For man is not from woman, but woman from man;
and man was not created for the sake of the woman, but woman for the sake of the man.
For this reason the woman ought to have authority over her head, because of the angels.

note.traditional: have a symbol of authority on her head

verse.note: Many versions supply “a symbol of” and take the phrase to mean a covering that marks the woman as under authority; those words are not in the Greek. Elsewhere the idiom “to have authority over” something means to have control of it, and it is rendered that way here: she is to exercise control over her head, presumably by keeping it covered. The traditional reading remains possible, and the verse is among the most disputed in the letter.

Paul does not explain this phrase. The most common proposal is that angels were thought to be present when the community worshiped and to care for its good order; another links it to the tradition, based on Genesis 6, of angels who desired human women. No explanation commands general agreement.

verse.text: Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not apart from man, nor man apart from woman.
For just as the woman is from the man, so also the man is through the woman; and all things are from God.
Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a woman to pray to God uncovered?
Does not nature itself teach you that if a man has long hair, it is a dishonor to him,
but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For long hair has been given as a covering.
verse.note: The preposition most often means “in place of,” which would make long hair itself the woman’s covering. It can also mean “as” or “answering to,” so that her hair is nature’s counterpart to the covering Paul asks for. Because verses 5–6 distinguish being uncovered from being shorn, most interpreters take it the second way, and the rendering leaves that open.

verse.text: But if anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor do the assemblies of God.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “church.” A first-century hearer knew this word as the term for a civic gathering and, from the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled before God; “church” now suggests a building or an institution. “Church” is near-universal in English versions and readers know what it refers to, but this translation uses “assembly” everywhere so that the one Greek word stays visible.

verse.text: In giving this instruction, however, I do not praise you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse.
For, in the first place, when you come together as an assembly, I hear that there are divisions among you, and in part I believe it.
For there must indeed be factions among you, so that those who are approved may become evident among you.
So when you come together in one place, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat,
for when it comes to eating, each of you goes ahead with your own supper, and one goes hungry while another gets drunk.
verse.note: The verb can mean “take beforehand,” implying that some began their meal before others, perhaps the poorer members, had arrived; it can also mean simply “consume,” with no idea of time. The matching instruction in verse 33 has the same ambiguity: “wait for one another” could also be “welcome one another.” The translation follows the temporal reading, which is the more common one.

verse.text: Do you really not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the assembly of God and shame those who have nothing? What should I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you.
For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night he was handed over, took bread,
verse.note: Most versions have “on the night he was betrayed.” The verb is the ordinary word for handing a person or thing into another’s control, and it is the same verb translated “handed on” earlier in this verse and in verse 2. “Betrayed” narrows the reference to Judas; “handed over” leaves room for the wider chain in which Jesus is handed over by Judas, by the authorities, and, in Paul’s own usage elsewhere, by God. Many scholars regard “betray” as an inference from context and not the word’s meaning, though others defend it here.

verse.text: and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said, “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”
verse.note: Many later manuscripts read “which is broken for you,” and that form passed into the King James Version and much liturgy; a few read “given.” Later manuscripts also add “Take, eat” before the saying. The earliest witnesses have only “which is for you,” and the longer forms are generally regarded as expansions.

verse.text: In the same way he also took the cup after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”
For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
So then, whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be answerable for the body and blood of the Lord.
Each person should examine themselves, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.
For whoever eats and drinks without judging the body rightly eats and drinks judgment on themselves.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “discerning the body.” The verb is a compound of “judge,” and in verses 29–32 Paul strings together a chain of related words (judgment, judge rightly, judged, condemned); the rendering keeps that chain audible. What “the body” means is disputed: the Lord’s body represented in the bread, or the gathered community as Christ’s body, whose poorer members were being shamed. Some later manuscripts add “unworthily” and “of the Lord.”

verse.text: That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a good number have fallen asleep.
verse.note: Sleep was a common euphemism for death, in Greek generally and especially among early Christians. Paul means that a number of the community have died, and he connects this with the abuses at the supper.

verse.text: But if we judged ourselves rightly, we would not be judged.
But when we are judged by the Lord, we are being disciplined, so that we may not be condemned along with the world.
So then, my brothers and sisters, when you come together to eat, wait for one another.
If anyone is hungry, they should eat at home, so that you do not come together for judgment. The rest I will set in order when I come.
Now about the things of the Spirit, brothers and sisters, I do not want you to be uninformed.
verse.note: The Greek is a bare adjective, “the spiritual,” with no noun. Most translations supply “gifts,” but the word for “gift” first appears in verse 4, so the broader phrase is used here.
