The form could also be masculine, “spiritual people,” meaning those who claimed special endowment by the Spirit; a minority of interpreters read it that way.

verse.text: You know that when you were Gentiles, you were carried off to idols that cannot speak, however you happened to be led.
verse.note: The Greek word means “nations” and, in the plural, the non-Jewish peoples; it is the same word translated “nations” elsewhere. Paul speaks as though his largely non-Jewish readers are no longer Gentiles, which is why many modern translations say “pagans” here.

verse.text: So I am making known to you that no one speaking by the Spirit of God says, “Jesus is accursed,” and no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except by the Holy Spirit.
verse.note: In the Greek Old Testament this word names something handed over to God for destruction, and so something under a curse. Why anyone would say this of Jesus is disputed: it may reflect rejection of a crucified Messiah, utterances in pagan worship, or simply a hypothetical opposite to the confession “Jesus is Lord.”

verse.text: There are different allotments of gifts, but the same Spirit;
verse.note: The noun can mean either “difference, variety” or “distribution, apportionment.” The related verb in verse 11 plainly means “distribute,” and this rendering keeps that link visible. Most translations prefer “varieties,” which is also lexically sound, and the contrast with “the same Spirit” implies variety on either reading.

verse.text: and there are different allotments of service, and the same Lord;
verse.note: The Greek word was an everyday term for service or for a task carried out on someone's behalf, not a religious office. “Ministry” now suggests clergy or a profession. Several modern translations also use “service” in this verse.

verse.text: and there are different allotments of workings, but the same God, who works all of them in everyone.
To each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good.
For to one a message of wisdom is given through the Spirit, to another a message of knowledge according to the same Spirit,
to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit,
to another workings of deeds of power, to another prophecy, to another the distinguishing of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues.
verse.note: The Greek is simply the plural of the ordinary word for “power,” used of concrete acts. “Miracles” is a fully acceptable rendering and the meaning is not in dispute. “Deeds of power” is used throughout this translation so that the connection with “power” stays visible.

The Greek word is the ordinary one for the tongue and for a language; a first-century reader would have heard “kinds of languages.” The traditional “tongues” is kept because it is the established name for this gift. Whether Paul means human languages unknown to the speaker or speech of another kind is debated.

verse.text: But one and the same Spirit works all these, allotting to each one individually just as he wills.
For just as the body is one and has many parts, and all the parts of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ.
verse.note: The Greek word means a limb or organ of a body. “Member” once meant exactly that in English, but now mainly suggests belonging to a club or organization, which blurs the bodily image Paul develops through the rest of the chapter.

verse.text: For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free—and we were all given one Spirit to drink.

note.traditional: by one Spirit; in one Spirit

verse.note: The Greek preposition can mark the Spirit as the element in which believers are baptized (“in”) or as the agent who baptizes (“by”). “In” is chosen because it matches the usual construction with “baptize” and fits the parallel image of drinking the Spirit. Many translations have “by.”

verse.text: For indeed the body is not one part but many.
If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” it does not for that reason stop belonging to the body.
And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” it does not for that reason stop belonging to the body.
If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the sense of smell be?
But as it is, God has placed the parts, each one of them, in the body just as he wanted.
If they were all one part, where would the body be?
But as it is, there are many parts, yet one body.
The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.”
On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are all the more necessary,
and the parts of the body we think less honorable we clothe with greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are made all the more presentable,
while our presentable parts have no such need. But God has composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacks it,
so that there may be no division in the body, but the parts may have the same concern for one another.
And if one part suffers, all the parts suffer with it; if one part is honored, all the parts rejoice with it.
Now you are the body of Christ, and individually parts of it.
And God has placed in the assembly first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then deeds of power, then gifts of healing, acts of help, acts of guidance, kinds of tongues.
verse.note: A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament's term for Israel assembled. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the one Greek word is always recognizable.

The word comes from the vocabulary of steering a ship. In the Greek Old Testament it is used for wise direction or counsel, as in Proverbs. Translations vary between “administration” and “leadership”; what activity Paul had in mind is not known in detail. Like the preceding term, it is plural in Greek and names activities, not offices.

verse.text: Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work deeds of power?
Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret?
But be eager for the greater gifts. And further, I will show you a way beyond all comparison.
verse.note: The Greek form can be a command (“be eager for”) or a statement (“you are eager for”). Most translations take it as a command, in line with the clear command using the same verb in 14:1. A minority read it as a description, even a mild rebuke, of the Corinthians' ambition, which Paul then answers with the “way” of chapter 13.

verse.text: If I speak in the tongues of humans and of angels but do not have love, I have become resounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a language as well as for the organ of speech. “Tongues” is kept here because it is the established English name for the gift of inspired speech that Paul discusses throughout chapters 12–14, but a first-century reader would have heard simply “the languages of humans and of angels.”

The Greek says only “bronze that makes a noise.” Most versions take this to be a gong; some scholars think instead of the bronze vessels used to amplify sound in theaters. Either way the image is of an object that produces sound without meaning.

verse.text: And if I have the gift of prophecy and know all the secrets and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing.
verse.note: In Jewish Greek of the period this word is the ordinary term for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose. English “mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, which is not the point. Most English versions keep “mysteries” as an established technical term, and many scholars defend that practice.

verse.text: And if I give away all I own to feed others, and if I hand over my body so that I may be burned, but do not have love, I gain nothing.

note.term: so that I may be burned

verse.note: The manuscripts are divided between two verbs that differ by a single letter in Greek. The SBLGNT, followed here, reads “so that I may be burned.” Several of the earliest manuscripts read “so that I may boast,” which the standard critical editions and a number of recent translations adopt. The question remains disputed.

verse.text: Love is patient; love is kind. Love does not envy; it does not brag, is not puffed up,
does not behave shamefully, does not seek its own interests, is not provoked to anger, keeps no account of wrongs,

note.traditional: thinketh no evil; is not resentful; keeps no record of wrongs

verse.note: The verb is a bookkeeping term meaning to reckon or enter in an account, and the object is literally “the evil.” The rendering takes this as not keeping a tally of injuries received, which is the majority view today. The phrase can also mean “does not plan evil,” as the older English versions understood it.

verse.text: does not rejoice at injustice, but rejoices with the truth.
It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
verse.note: The verb can mean either “bear, put up with” or “cover, protect,” and both senses are attested in the period. Paul’s other uses (1 Corinthians 9:12; 1 Thessalonians 3:1, 5) favor “bear,” but “covers all things,” meaning love shields others or keeps silent about their faults, is a serious alternative. The repeated “all things” can also be read adverbially, “always” or “in everything.”

verse.text: Love never fails. But as for prophecies, they will be done away with; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will be done away with.
verse.note: Paul uses the same verb four times in verses 8–11, of prophecies, knowledge, the partial, and the ways of a child. It means to put something out of operation or bring it to an end. Many versions vary the English (“pass away,” “come to an end,” “give up”); one rendering is kept here so the repetition can be heard.

verse.text: For we know in part and we prophesy in part;
but when what is complete comes, what is in part will be done away with.

note.traditional: the perfect; that which is perfect

verse.note: The word means whole, full-grown or having reached its goal, and here it stands in direct contrast with “what is in part.” “Complete” keeps that contrast, where “perfect” might suggest moral flawlessness. The traditional rendering is “the perfect,” though several modern versions also have “the complete” or “completeness.”

verse.text: When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I did away with the ways of a child.
For now we see in a mirror, as in a riddle, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, just as I too have been fully known.
verse.note: The Greek says “in a riddle,” that is, in an indirect or puzzling form. The wording echoes Numbers 12:8 in the Greek Old Testament, where God speaks with Moses “mouth to mouth” and “not in riddles.” The traditional “dimly” or “darkly” suggests a poor reflection, but the point is more likely that a mirror gives only an indirect view compared with seeing face to face. Ancient mirrors were of polished metal.

verse.text: And now faith, hope, love remain—these three; and the greatest of these is love.
verse.note: The phrase can be temporal (“at the present time”) or logical (“as things stand”). On the first reading faith, hope and love remain during the present age; on the second all three endure, in contrast with the gifts that will be done away with. Interpreters are divided. “Greatest” renders a Greek comparative, “greater,” which commonly served for the superlative in this period.

verse.text: Pursue love, and be eager for the spiritual gifts, but even more that you may prophesy.
For the one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to people but to God, for no one understands; rather, in the spirit he speaks secrets.
verse.note: In Jewish Greek of the period this is the ordinary word for a secret, especially something known to God and not disclosed. Modern “mystery” suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding. Most English versions keep “mysteries” as an established term. Here the point is simply that what is said stays hidden from the hearers.

The Greek has no article and could mean the speaker’s own spirit or the Holy Spirit (“by the Spirit”). The lowercase reading is chosen because verse 14 speaks of “my spirit” praying in contrast with “my mind.” Many translations and commentators prefer “in the Spirit,” and Paul may not have drawn the line sharply.

verse.text: But the one who prophesies speaks to people for building up and encouragement and comfort.
The one who speaks in a tongue builds himself up, but the one who prophesies builds up the assembly.
verse.note: A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled. “Church” is near-universal in English Bibles and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. In this chapter Paul has the actual gathered meeting in view.

verse.text: I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more that you may prophesy. The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets, so that the assembly may receive building up.
But now, brothers and sisters, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I speak to you with a revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?
verse.note: The Greek plural was regularly used to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is addressing the whole community. Several modern versions also render it “brothers and sisters”; others keep “brothers” and explain the inclusive sense in a footnote.

verse.text: Even lifeless things that give a sound, whether pipe or lyre—if they make no distinction between the notes, how will anyone know what is being played on the pipe or the lyre?
And if the trumpet gives an unclear sound, who will get ready for battle?
So it is with you: unless you give intelligible speech with your tongue, how will anyone know what is being said? You will be speaking into the air.
There are who knows how many kinds of languages in the world, and none is without meaning.
So if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker, and the speaker a foreigner to me.
So it is with you: since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, seek to abound in them for the building up of the assembly.
verse.note: The Greek says literally “eager for spirits.” Most interpreters take the plural as shorthand for the Spirit’s various workings, as in 12:7–11, and translations give “spiritual gifts” or “manifestations of the Spirit.” A minority think Paul is echoing the Corinthians’ own way of speaking about spirit-powers.

verse.text: Therefore let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret.
For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful.
What then? I will pray with the spirit, but I will also pray with the mind; I will sing with the spirit, but I will also sing with the mind.
Otherwise, if you speak a blessing in the spirit, how will the one who fills the place of the uninstructed say “Amen” to your thanksgiving, since that person does not know what you are saying?
verse.note: The Greek word means a layperson or non-expert as opposed to someone trained. Here it may be anyone in the meeting who cannot understand the tongue. Or it may be a distinct group, such as interested inquirers who are not yet believers, as verses 23–24 may suggest. Translations vary among “outsider,” “inquirer,” “ungifted” and “uninformed”; one neutral word is used in all three verses to leave the question open.

verse.text: You, to be sure, are giving thanks well, but the other person is not being built up.
I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you;
but in the assembly I would rather speak five words with my mind, so as to instruct others also, than ten thousand words in a tongue.
Brothers and sisters, do not be children in your thinking. In evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature.
In the Law it is written: “By people of other tongues and by the lips of others I will speak to this people, and not even so will they listen to me, says the Lord.”

note.term: In the Law it is written:

verse.note: The quotation is a free citation of Isaiah 28:11–12, where God warns Israel that, since they would not listen to plain speech, he will address them through the foreign language of invaders. Paul uses “the Law” broadly here for Scripture as a whole, not only the books of Moses. The same broad use may lie behind verse 34, where no specific passage is cited.

verse.text: So then, tongues serve as a sign not for those who believe but for unbelievers, while prophecy is not for unbelievers but for those who believe.
So if the whole assembly comes together in one place and all speak in tongues, and uninstructed people or unbelievers come in, will they not say that you are out of your minds?
But if all prophesy, and some unbeliever or uninstructed person comes in, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all,
the hidden things of his heart are brought to light, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring, “God is truly among you!”
What then, brothers and sisters? When you come together, each one has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has a tongue, has an interpretation. Let everything be done for building up.
If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be two or at most three, each in turn, and let one person interpret.
But if there is no interpreter, let the speaker be silent in the assembly and speak to himself and to God.
Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said.
But if something is revealed to another who is sitting there, let the first be silent.
For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged
(and the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets,
for God is not a God of disorder but of peace), as in all the assemblies of the holy ones.
verse.note: The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament’s language for Israel. “Saints,” which many translations keep, now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Other versions use “God’s people.”

note.term: as in all the assemblies of the holy ones

verse.note: This phrase can be attached to what precedes, as here, following the punctuation of the SBLGNT, so that orderly prophecy is the practice of all the assemblies. Many translations instead begin a new sentence with it: “As in all the assemblies of the holy ones, let the women be silent.” The Greek allows either, and the choice affects how general the instruction in verse 34 sounds.

verse.text: Let the women be silent in the assemblies, for they are not permitted to speak; rather, let them be subject, as the Law also says.

note.term: Let the women be silent in the assemblies

verse.note: A few manuscripts, chiefly of the Western tradition, place verses 34–35 after verse 40. Partly for that reason, and because of the tension with 11:5 where women pray and prophesy, some scholars judge the two verses a later marginal comment that entered the text. Most editors and translations keep them here, since no surviving manuscript omits them. The SBLGNT prints them without brackets.

The Greek word means both “woman” and “wife,” and verse 35’s reference to “their own husbands” suggests married women are particularly in view. How far the silence extends is disputed. Since 11:5 assumes women pray and prophesy, many interpreters take it to restrict a particular kind of speaking, such as questioning or evaluating prophecies, and not all speech. Others read it as a general rule.

verse.text: If there is something they want to learn, let them ask their own husbands at home, for it is shameful for a woman to speak in the assembly.
Or did the word of God go out from you? Or has it reached only you?
If anyone thinks he is a prophet or a spiritual person, let him recognize that what I am writing to you is from the Lord.

note.traditional: is a command of the Lord

verse.note: Many manuscripts read “is a command of the Lord” or “are commands of the Lord,” and most English versions follow them. The SBLGNT adopts the shorter reading, without the word “command,” found in some witnesses. The sense is little affected.

verse.text: But if anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized.
verse.note: Other manuscripts have an imperative, “let him be ignorant,” which the KJV follows. The reading translated here is a passive, which may mean not recognized by God or not recognized by the assembly as a prophet or spiritual person. The Greek plays on the verb “recognize” in verse 37.

verse.text: So then, my brothers and sisters, be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues;
but let everything be done decently and in order.
Now I make known to you, brothers and sisters, the good news that I announced to you, which you also received, in which you also stand,
verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. “Gospel” now sounds like a religious term or the title of a book. Many modern translations alternate between the two; the related verb in verses 1 and 2 is rendered “announced” with “good news.”

verse.text: and through which you are also being saved, if you hold fast to the message with which I announced the good news to you—unless you believed in vain.
For I handed on to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures,
and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures,
and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve.
After that he appeared to more than five hundred brothers and sisters at one time, most of whom remain until now, though some have fallen asleep.
After that he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.
Last of all, as if to a miscarried child, he appeared to me as well.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a miscarriage or stillbirth, as in the Greek versions of Numbers 12:12 and Job 3:16; it does not mean a late birth. Most translations soften it to “one untimely born” or “abnormally born.” What Paul intends by the image is debated: it may be a term of abuse he is taking over from critics, or a picture of the violent and irregular way he became an apostle.

verse.text: For I am the least of the apostles, not fit to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God.
verse.note: A first-century hearer knew this word as the term for a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament’s word for Israel assembled. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is always visible.

verse.text: But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me did not prove empty; on the contrary, I labored harder than all of them—though not I, but the grace of God that is with me.
So whether it was I or they, this is what we proclaim and this is what you believed.
Now if Christ is proclaimed as having been raised from the dead, how can some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?
If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised either;
and if Christ has not been raised, then our proclamation is empty, and your faith is empty too.
We are also found to be false witnesses about God, because we testified against God that he raised Christ—whom he did not raise, if in fact the dead are not raised.
For if the dead are not raised, then Christ has not been raised either;
and if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins.
Then those who have fallen asleep in Christ have also perished.
If our hope in Christ is for this life only, we are more to be pitied than all other people.

note.traditional: If in this life only we have hope in Christ

verse.note: The word “only” stands at the end of the Greek clause. It may limit “in this life,” as rendered here and in most translations, or it may qualify the whole clause: “if in this life we have done nothing more than hope in Christ.” Either way the point is that a hope with no resurrection behind it is pitiable.

verse.text: But as it is, Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.
For since death came through a human, the resurrection of the dead has also come through a human.
verse.note: The Greek word means a human being, not specifically a male, and Paul’s argument turns on Adam and Christ each standing for humanity. The same rendering is kept in verses 45 and 47, where translations traditionally have “the first man” and “the second man.” Some recent versions likewise use “human being” here.

verse.text: For just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.
But each in the proper order: Christ the firstfruits; then, at his coming, those who belong to Christ;
verse.note: The Greek word means arrival and presence. In Paul’s world it was the regular term for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city, and a first-century reader would have heard that royal overtone here.

verse.text: then the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when he has abolished every rule and every authority and power.
verse.note: Many translations have “destroyed” here and in verse 26. The Greek verb is not the ordinary word for destroying; it means to put out of operation or bring to an end, and the lexicons give “abolish” among its senses. The same English word is used in both verses so that the repetition is heard.

verse.text: For he must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet.
The last enemy to be abolished is death,
for “he has subjected all things under his feet.” But when it says that all things have been subjected, it is clear that this excludes the one who subjected all things to him.
And when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all.
Otherwise, what will those people do who are baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are they baptized on their behalf?

note.term: baptized on behalf of the dead

verse.note: The plain sense of the Greek is that some people were being baptized on behalf of people who had died, and most scholars read it that way, though nothing else is known of such a practice in Paul’s time. Many other explanations have been proposed and none has won general agreement. Paul neither commends nor condemns the practice; he appeals to it only as evidence that those who do it expect the dead to be raised.

verse.text: And why do we ourselves face danger every hour?
I die every day—I swear it by my boasting in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord.
If I fought wild beasts in Ephesus from merely human motives, what good is that to me? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
verse.note: The verb is the term for fighting animals in the arena. Most scholars take it here as a figure for violent human opposition in Ephesus, since Paul gives no hint elsewhere of having survived the arena, but a literal sense cannot be ruled out. The saying that closes the verse is from Isaiah 22:13.

verse.text: Do not be led astray: “Bad company ruins good character.”
verse.note: This is a line of Greek verse, usually attributed to the comic playwright Menander, which by Paul’s time circulated as a proverb. The word rendered “company” can also mean “conversation.”

verse.text: Sober up, as you rightly should, and stop sinning; for some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.
But someone will say, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?”
Fool! What you yourself sow is not made alive unless it dies.
And as for what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of something else.
But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each of the seeds its own body.
Not all flesh is the same flesh: there is one for humans, another flesh for animals, another flesh for birds, and another for fish.
There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but the glory of the heavenly is one kind, and that of the earthly is another.
The sun has one glory, the moon another glory, and the stars another glory; for star differs from star in glory.
So it is with the resurrection of the dead. It is sown perishable; it is raised imperishable.
It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual one.
verse.note: “Natural” and “spiritual” translate adjectives formed from the Greek words for the life of a living creature and for spirit, the same pair that appears in verse 45 as “living being” and “life-giving spirit.” Most scholars hold that the contrast is between a body animated by ordinary life and a body animated by the Spirit, not between a material body and an immaterial one. English cannot show the verbal link, so the traditional pair is kept. The quotation in verse 45 is Genesis 2:7, to which Paul adds “first” and “Adam.”

verse.text: So also it is written: “The first human, Adam, became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit.
But the spiritual is not first; the natural is, and then the spiritual.
The first human was from the earth, made of dust; the second human is from heaven.
As the one made of dust was, so also are those made of dust; and as the heavenly one is, so also are the heavenly ones.
And just as we have borne the image of the one made of dust, we will also bear the image of the heavenly one.
verse.note: Many early and important manuscripts read “let us also bear,” an exhortation, which differs from “we will also bear” by a single vowel that was pronounced alike. The Greek text followed here prints the future, as do most modern translations, on the ground that the passage is describing what will happen, not urging conduct. A number of scholars prefer the better-attested exhortation.

verse.text: What I am saying, brothers and sisters, is this: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable.
Look, I am telling you a secret: we will not all fall asleep, but we will all be changed,
verse.note: In Jewish Greek of the period this was the ordinary word for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose. Most English versions keep “mystery” as an established term for a truth once hidden and now revealed. “Secret” is used here because “mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas Paul goes straight on to state the matter plainly.

verse.text: in an instant, in the blink of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed.
For this perishable body must put on imperishability, and this mortal body must put on immortality.
And when this perishable body has put on imperishability and this mortal body has put on immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.”

text.q: “Where, death, is your victory? Where, death, is your sting?”

verse.text: The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.
But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
So then, my beloved brothers and sisters, be steadfast, immovable, always overflowing in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not empty.
Now concerning the collection for the holy ones: just as I directed the assemblies of Galatia, so you also are to do.
verse.note: This is the fund Paul was gathering from his largely non-Jewish assemblies for the impoverished believers in Jerusalem. He also discusses it in Romans 15 and 2 Corinthians 8–9. The Greek word was an ordinary term for a collection of money, often for a religious purpose.

The traditional rendering is “saints,” which now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Paul uses the word for all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Here it refers specifically to the believers in Jerusalem. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

The traditional rendering is “churches.” A first-century hearer knew this word as the ordinary term for a civic gathering and as the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled, whereas “church” now suggests a building or an institution. “Church” remains near-universal in English translations, and some find that “assembly” sounds like a one-off meeting.

verse.text: On the first day of every week, each of you is to set something aside and save it up at home, in proportion to how you have prospered, so that no collections have to be made when I come.

note.term: On the first day of every week
note.traditional: Upon the first day of the week

verse.note: The Greek follows the Jewish way of counting days from the Sabbath, so the day meant is Sunday. This is one of the earliest indications that the first day of the week had special significance for believers. The instruction itself, however, is about each person setting money aside privately, not about an offering taken at a meeting.

verse.text: And when I arrive, I will send those you approve, with letters, to carry your gift to Jerusalem.

note.traditional: whomsoever ye shall approve by your letters, them will I send

verse.note: The phrase can attach to either verb. On the reading adopted here, Paul will send the approved delegates with letters of introduction; on the other, the Corinthians approve their delegates by letter. Most modern translations take the first view, since Paul would be present in Corinth and written approval from the Corinthians would be unnecessary.

verse.text: And if it is worthwhile for me to go as well, they will go with me.
I will come to you after I pass through Macedonia—for I am going through Macedonia—
and perhaps I will stay with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me on my way wherever I go.
For I do not want to see you now only in passing; I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits.
But I will remain in Ephesus until Pentecost,
for a great and effective door has opened for me, and there are many who oppose me.
If Timothy comes, see that he can be with you without fear, for he is doing the Lord’s work, just as I am.
So let no one treat him with contempt. Send him on his way in peace, so that he may come to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers.
Now concerning our brother Apollos: I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers, but he was not at all willing to come now; he will come when he has the opportunity.

note.term: he was not at all willing
note.traditional: his will was not at all to come at this time

verse.note: The Greek says only “it was not at all the will that he come now,” without saying whose will. Most translations take it as Apollos’s own unwillingness, which fits the following clause about his finding an opportunity. Some interpreters take it as God’s will, since the word used without qualification can have that sense.

verse.text: Stay alert, stand firm in the faith, be courageous, be strong.
verse.note: The verb is formed from the word for “man,” and older translations render it “quit you like men” or “act like men.” In period usage, and repeatedly in the Septuagint alongside “be strong,” it simply means to show courage, and it is addressed here to the whole community. Several modern translations render it the same way.

verse.text: Let everything you do be done in love.
Now I urge you, brothers and sisters—you know the household of Stephanas, that they are the firstfruits of Achaia and that they have devoted themselves to the service of the holy ones—
verse.note: The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the normal way to address a mixed group of siblings or fellow members, and Paul is addressing the whole community, women included. Where the word refers to specific traveling companions (verses 11 and 12), “brothers” is kept. Some translations retain “brothers” throughout and explain the inclusive sense in a footnote.

Many translations have “ministry” here. In the first century this was an everyday word for serving someone or carrying out a task on another’s behalf, and it did not denote a religious office. “Ministry” now suggests clergy or a church profession. Some translations also use “service” in this verse.

verse.text: that you too submit to such people, and to everyone who shares in the work and labors at it.
I rejoice at the arrival of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence,
verse.note: This is the same Greek word used elsewhere for the “coming” of the Lord. Here it has its everyday sense of someone arriving and being present. “Arrival” is used for ordinary people to keep the two uses distinct.

verse.text: for they have refreshed my spirit and yours. So give such people recognition.
The assemblies of Asia greet you. Aquila and Prisca greet you warmly in the Lord, together with the assembly that meets in their house.
All the brothers and sisters greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss.
This greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s.
verse.note: Letters were normally dictated to a secretary. At this point Paul takes the pen himself and writes the closing lines, a common practice that served as a personal mark of authenticity.

verse.text: If anyone does not love the Lord, let that person be accursed. Our Lord, come!
verse.note: Paul writes an Aramaic phrase in Greek letters without translating it, evidently a cry already familiar from the worship of the earliest Aramaic-speaking believers. Divided as “marana tha” it is a prayer, “Our Lord, come!”; divided as “maran atha” it would be a statement, “Our Lord has come.” Most scholars favor the prayer, which matches “Come, Lord Jesus” in Revelation 22:20. Older translations leave the phrase untranslated as “Maranatha.”

verse.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you.
My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus.
